I have been farming this land for 25 years, and I know what works here in Quzhou County. With 8 mu of good flat land and a well for irrigation, I stick to the wheat-maize double-cropping system that feeds my household of seven. Some of my family works off-farm, so I cannot afford to waste labor or time. I plant the whole 8 mu to winter wheat in October, harvest it in early June, and immediately put in summer maize on the same 8 mu. That is how we get two crops from one piece of land each year.

For the winter wheat, I will rotary till the soil before sowing and use an improved local wheat variety — the same kind my neighbors use, because I trust what I see in the fields around me. I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dose and then topdress with urea in spring when the wheat greens up. Wheat needs water at key stages, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once at jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling if the weather turns dry. I will spray herbicide once after sowing and use insecticide or fungicide twice if I see aphids or rust starting.

For the summer maize, time is short between wheat harvest and planting, so I will plant directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage to save labor and catch the season. Everyone here grows hybrid maize now — the yields are much better than the old types. I will apply compound fertilizer at planting and add urea when the maize is knee-high. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, but I will irrigate twice: once around the jointing stage and again at silking, because that is when the kernels set. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice, especially if the corn borer shows up.

I expect about 500 kg per mu of wheat and a bit more than 500 kg per mu of maize if the weather cooperates. I do not chase record yields — I aim for steady, reliable harvests that cover my family’s grain needs and leave some to sell.
